newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt must update finance sector - expert.
newsitem.headline: Egypt must update finance sector - expert.

text.p: A leading financial expert said on Monday Egypt must sustain its economic reform programme and particularly its financial system to become one of the leading emerging markets of the world.

Charles Dallara, managing director of the Institute of International Finance (IIF), told reporters in Cairo that he was encouraged by the accelerated reforms but that Egypt must keep it up to continue to attract investors.

"It's important that the government must not believe its own headlines," Dallara told Reuters. "It's easy to think that success has come and then rest on your laurels." The IIF is a global association of private financial institutions.
"Egypt has a long way to go and it started late, so the rate of reform must be rapid because markets are fickle," he added.
After years of stalling, Egypt's privatisation-led reforms only really took off in January 1996 after President Hosni Mubarak appointed a more economically minded cabinet.

The faster pace, as well as a recent investment grade credit rating by international agency Standard & Poor's, has drawn millions of dollars in portfolio investment into Egypt, estimated by the International Monetary Fund at $600 million in the first half of the 1996/7 financial year. It has overtaken direct investment, forecast at $800 million in the whole year.

The capital inflows have helped fuel a month-long record run on the bourse, whose the all-share index rose by almost 34 percent since the beginning of the year. In the whole of 1996, the index increased 39 percent.

Egyptian officials and the goverment-run press have been touting the recent reforms as Egypt's answer to the Asian "tiger" developing economies but Dallara said that Egypt still needed to work on sustaining global interest.
"Egypt is still a relatively small player in the global picture and encouraged as I am by the reforms and the clear programme, I am calling for sustainability to ensure their full benefits," he said.
Dallara said that most of the $231 billion of private capital which poured into emerging markets in 1996 went to Latin America and Asia but the Middle East's share was tiny.
"Investors are looking for places to put their money with the most benefit. I think Egypt and the region could benefit from more reforms," he said.

Dallara said that Egypt needed to attract more direct foreign investment, as opposed to "hot money" which flows in and out at the least sign of instability. Egypt needed to remove some barriers like complicated labour laws, further trade liberalisation and also update its commercial code.

Cairo could also expand its barely visible debt market and streamline its banking sector so that it stands up to foreign competition, Dallara and Mahmoud Abdel Aziz, head of the Egyptian Banking Federation, told reporters.

"Developing the banking sector is key to a healthy financial system," Dallara said. "And we're quite encouraged by the developments in the banking sector but it needs more efficiency, more risk management, newer technology and trained personnel."

"We also need more capitalisation, privatisation, transparency and an update of the banking functions. As it is, banks have a monopoly on financial life in Egypt," said Abdel Aziz, who is chairman of the country's largest state-run bank the National Bank of Egypt.

The state has already asked public banks to sell their stakes in joint venture banks and the sub-governor of the Central Bank said that Egypt would privatise one of its main four retail banks by the end of the year.
